summary:
The challenge is that people are not always good at noticing changes in their own health. Some changes take time to be noticed, and by the time a message reaches the earth (up to 22 minutes from Mars), it might be too late. 

That’s where the SecOp comes in, it is a 5-minute health exam that allows each member of the crew to perform health checks on each other. SecOp consists of 5 different stations to perform a basic health exam: Using the camera to assess the pupil reflex; Placing a fingertip on the camera to take a heart rate reading (seated and standing); Using the motion sensor to perform a basic balance test; Quick tests to assess sleep, mood and a the last, a reaction time test. Each station is guided by a voice prompt, as well as control buttons. Rather than comparing the results to a large population, SecOp compares the results to the person’s previous exams. Any concerning results are flagged to the user, and includes the next steps, as outlined in NASA’s ISS Medical Checklist on what to do and when to contact the flight surgeon. 

Results are stored on the device, and can be transferred to another device using a QR code. SecOp runs offline on a phone/tablet that is already being sent up with the crew.
details:
SecOp is a 5 minute peer health assessment. This can be done by one crewmate using the existing phone/tablet. There are 5 sections.

Pupil Check: Using the camera the pupil will be focused on. The screen goes dark then flashes white OR the flash goes off. This shows how fast and how much your pupils constrict.

Heart Rate: Put your fingertip on the back camera and turn on the flashlight. Heart rate will be taken whilst sitting and standing. This can show an increase due to re-adapting to gravity.

Balance: Stand with feet together, close your eyes and hold the phone to your chest. A motion sensor will measure your balance.

Sleep & Mood: Answer some quick questions.

Reaction Times: Tap the screen when it turns green. Based on the PVT-B reaction time test.

The first two tests form a baseline. All results will be compared against these. If there is any change such as an increase in heart rate of 30bpm when standing or slower reaction times by 20%, an action card will be generated from the NASA ISS Medical Checklist. The result card will show in real-time the light delay between Mars and Earth using NASA JPL Orbital data. Each individual will have their own trends page and results can be moved to another phone using a QR code.

Benefits

Can help detect small changes. No extra equipment required. Can be used fully offline.

During a Mars mission the crew are responsible for their own care. Communication can take up to 22 mins to reach Earth. This quick test can help identify any issues. The flight surgeon will have a history of each individual. Could be used in Moon bases, Analog missions, Antarctic stations and remote healthcare workers.

Technologies

This is a web app built using Next.js, React, Typescript and TailwindCSS. Data is stored locally on the device using IndexedDB. A service worker makes it possible to use it offline. MediaPipe from Google is used to track the eye. The AI voice prompts have been recorded once using Groq’s Orpheus. The app has been tested using Vitest and is hosted on Vercel. Claude Code was used to help with writing the code. The wearable part of the app is optional. A consumer band is used with the Google Health API.

Creativity

The app utilises the crewmate to do the assessment. The astronauts do not need to assess themselves. The phone acts as a pupillometer, pulse monitor and balance board. Everyone will be compared to their own baseline. We suggest a new light-weight wearable to be worn throughout the day. This will monitor the heart (ECG) and send data to the crews tablet via a wired connection. We have used a consumer band in our prototype.

Considerations

No internet required. No extra weight. Sections relating to gravity will not be used in space. No AI diagnosis. Easy to measure. Actions are based on NASA processes and are decided by the flight surgeon. If sensors fail the examiner can manually score. Pupil tests work best in bright lighting and lighter eyes. Data from examination is stored on the crews devices. Big buttons and easy to read font. Voice prompts can be turned off.

Prototype created during a hackathon. Not validated for clinical use.
